questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question_text: A 24-year-old man sustains an anterior shoulder dislocation while playing rugby. After closed reduction, he is unable to abduct his arm beyond 15 degrees and has lost sensation over the 'regimental badge' area of the lateral shoulder. Which nerve is most likely injured?

options.A: Radial nerve
options.B: Axillary nerve
options.C: Musculocutaneous nerve
options.D: Suprascapular nerve

questions.explanation: The axillary nerve (C5, C6) winds around the surgical neck of the humerus and is the nerve most commonly injured in anterior shoulder dislocation or surgical neck fracture. It supplies deltoid and teres minor, and its cutaneous branch supplies the 'regimental badge' area over the lower deltoid.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question_text: During a left total thyroidectomy, the surgeon ligates the inferior thyroid artery close to the gland to minimise risk of nerve injury. The recurrent laryngeal nerve has a closer relationship to the inferior thyroid artery on which side, and why is this side at greater surgical risk overall?

options.A: Right side — the right RLN crosses the artery superficially and is shorter, looping around the subclavian artery
options.B: Left side — the left RLN is longer, loops around the aortic arch, and ascends in the tracheoesophageal groove closely related to the artery
options.C: Both sides are equally at risk with no anatomical difference
options.D: Neither nerve relates to the inferior thyroid artery

questions.explanation: The left recurrent laryngeal nerve loops around the arch of the aorta and ascends in the tracheoesophageal groove, running in close proximity to the inferior thyroid artery throughout its course — making meticulous identification essential during thyroidectomy. The right RLN has a more oblique, shorter course around the subclavian artery.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question_text: A 60-year-old male with end-stage renal disease on dialysis is found on chest X-ray to have a dilated inferior vena cava at the diaphragm. At which vertebral level does the IVC pass through the diaphragm, and through which part of the diaphragm?

options.A: T8, through the central tendon
options.B: T10, through the right crus
options.C: T12, through the muscular part
options.D: T9, through the left crus

questions.explanation: The caval opening lies in the central tendon of the diaphragm at the level of T8, transmitting the IVC and the right phrenic nerve. The oesophageal hiatus is at T10 (right crus muscle), and the aortic hiatus is at T12 (behind the diaphragm, transmitting aorta, thoracic duct, and azygos vein).

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question_text: A patient with a fractured mandible develops weakness of jaw closure with deviation of the jaw to the unaffected side on attempted opening. Which group of muscles is most likely affected, and which nerve supplies them?

options.A: Muscles of facial expression — facial nerve (CN VII)
options.B: Muscles of mastication (masseter, temporalis, pterygoids) — mandibular division of trigeminal nerve (CN V3)
options.C: Suprahyoid muscles — ansa cervicalis
options.D: Buccinator — facial nerve (CN VII)

questions.explanation: The muscles of mastication — masseter, temporalis, medial and lateral pterygoid — are all supplied by CN V3 (mandibular division of trigeminal nerve). The lateral pterygoid protrudes and depresses the mandible; unilateral weakness causes deviation toward the weak side on opening. Buccinator aids chewing but is a muscle of facial expression supplied by CN VII, not mastication.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question_text: During a laparoscopic cholecystectomy, the surgeon is dissecting Calot's triangle to identify the cystic artery before clipping it. What are the boundaries of Calot's triangle?

options.A: Cystic duct (inferolaterally), common hepatic duct (medially), inferior border of the liver (superiorly)
options.B: Cystic artery, common bile duct, and right hepatic artery
options.C: Gallbladder fundus, hepatoduodenal ligament, and portal vein
options.D: Common bile duct, gastroduodenal artery, and pancreas

questions.explanation: Calot's (hepatocystic) triangle is bounded by the cystic duct inferolaterally, the common hepatic duct medially, and the inferior border of the liver superiorly. The cystic artery (usually from the right hepatic artery) lies within this triangle and must be positively identified before division to avoid bile duct injury.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question_text: A 29-year-old man falls asleep with his arm draped over the back of a chair after heavy alcohol intake. The next morning, he has wrist drop and cannot extend his fingers, but triceps strength is normal. Where is the lesion, and why is triceps spared?

options.A: Radial nerve in the axilla — triceps branch arises distally
options.B: Radial nerve in the spiral groove of the humerus — the triceps branch arises proximal to the groove
options.C: Posterior interosseous nerve at the supinator — triceps is not supplied by the radial nerve
options.D: C7 nerve root — triceps is supplied by C8 only

questions.explanation: This is 'Saturday night palsy' — radial nerve compression in the spiral groove of the humerus from prolonged pressure (e.g., arm draped over a hard edge). The branch to triceps arises proximal to the spiral groove, so triceps strength is preserved while wrist and finger extensors (supplied distal to the groove) are weak, producing wrist drop.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question_text: A neonate with DiGeorge syndrome (22q11.2 deletion) is found to have a single great vessel arising from the heart, overriding both ventricles, with a large VSD beneath it. Echocardiography confirms the diagnosis shown. Failure of which embryological process explains this anomaly?

options.A: Failure of endocardial cushion fusion
options.B: Failure of the aorticopulmonary (truncoconal) septum to spiral and divide the truncus arteriosus
options.C: Failure of atrial septum primum resorption
options.D: Failure of the ductus arteriosus to close

questions.explanation: Persistent truncus arteriosus results from failure of neural-crest-derived aorticopulmonary septal tissue to grow and spiral, leaving a single arterial trunk supplying both the systemic and pulmonary circulations, with an obligatory VSD. It is strongly associated with 22q11.2 deletion (DiGeorge syndrome), reflecting the neural crest origin of the conotruncal septum.
key_findings: A single large arterial trunk arises from the heart, overriding both ventricles
A large ventricular septal defect is seen immediately beneath the single vessel
No separate pulmonary trunk is identified arising independently from the right ventricle
Both great vessels of a normal heart (aorta and pulmonary trunk) cannot be separately traced

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question_text: A patient undergoes a femoral hernia repair. The surgeon identifies the femoral canal medial to the femoral vein. Which structure forms the medial boundary of the femoral ring, making it a classic site of incarceration?

options.A: Inguinal ligament
options.B: Lacunar ligament
options.C: Pectineal ligament
options.D: Femoral sheath

questions.explanation: The femoral ring is bounded anteriorly by the inguinal ligament, posteriorly by the pectineal ligament, laterally by the femoral vein, and medially by the sharp, unyielding lacunar ligament. This rigid medial margin is why femoral hernias have a high risk of strangulation — the lacunar ligament cannot stretch to relieve compression on herniated bowel.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question_text: On a contrast CT, the gallbladder fossa is identified between two hepatic segments using the Couinaud classification. Which two segments border the gallbladder fossa?

options.A: Segments I and II
options.B: Segments III and VI
options.C: Segments IV and V
options.D: Segments VII and VIII

questions.explanation: In the Couinaud segmental classification, the gallbladder fossa lies between segment IV (part of the left lobe) and segment V (part of the right lobe). Segment I is the caudate lobe, lying posteriorly between the IVC groove and the porta hepatis.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question_text: A 2-year-old presents with painless rectal bleeding. A technetium-99m pertechnetate scan shows uptake in the right lower abdomen corresponding to ectopic gastric mucosa. This is a Meckel's diverticulum. It is a remnant of which embryological structure?

options.A: Urachus
options.B: Vitelline (omphalomesenteric) duct
options.C: Allantois
options.D: Umbilical vein

questions.explanation: Meckel's diverticulum is a true diverticulum resulting from incomplete obliteration of the vitelline (omphalomesenteric) duct, typically found within 2 feet of the ileocaecal valve, 2 inches long, and may contain ectopic gastric or pancreatic tissue ('rule of 2s'). The technetium scan detects ectopic gastric mucosa secreting acid that causes painless bleeding.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question_text: A patient with a supracondylar fracture of the humerus develops a claw-like deformity of the hand with hyperextension at the MCP joints and flexion at the IP joints of the ring and little fingers, sparing the thumb. Sensory loss is present over the medial 1.5 digits. Which nerve injury, and at what level relative to the elbow, best explains this?

options.A: Median nerve at the wrist (carpal tunnel)
options.B: Ulnar nerve proximal to the forearm, sparing flexor digitorum profundus to the ring/little fingers and flexor carpi ulnaris
options.C: Radial nerve in the spiral groove
options.D: Ulnar nerve at the wrist (Guyon's canal), with intact forearm branches

questions.explanation: This is a classic 'ulnar paradox': ulnar nerve injury at the wrist (distal lesion, e.g., Guyon's canal) produces a MORE pronounced claw hand than a proximal lesion, because the flexor digitorum profundus to the ring/little fingers (innervated proximally) remains intact and continues to flex the IP joints unopposed by the now-paralysed lumbricals, while the paralysed interossei/lumbricals fail to flex the MCP joints — producing hyperextension at MCP and flexion at IP joints. A proximal ulnar lesion paralyses FDP too, reducing the clawing.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question_text: A 50-year-old male presents with a painless midline neck swelling that moves upward on tongue protrusion. The ultrasound shown confirms a cystic lesion. This is a thyroglossal duct cyst. From which embryological site does the thyroid gland originate before its descent?

options.A: First pharyngeal pouch
options.B: Foramen caecum, at the junction of the anterior two-thirds and posterior one-third of the tongue
options.C: Second branchial arch
options.D: Rathke's pouch

questions.explanation: The thyroid gland arises as an endodermal downgrowth from the foramen caecum at the tongue base and descends through the neck via the thyroglossal duct, passing close to or through the hyoid bone, to reach its final pretracheal position by week 7. Failure of the duct to obliterate leaves a thyroglossal duct cyst anywhere along this path, classically moving with tongue protrusion due to its attachment to the duct remnant.
key_findings: A well-defined anechoic cystic lesion is seen in the midline neck, just below the hyoid bone
The lesion is closely related to the hyoid bone with no clear separation
No solid or vascular component is identified within the cyst
The thyroid gland in its normal pretracheal position appears unremarkable

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question_text: A patient with a posterior MI develops sinus bradycardia and first-degree AV block. Coronary angiography shows occlusion of a dominant right coronary artery proximal to its main branch points. Which structures explain both findings?

options.A: Left anterior descending artery supplies the SA node only
options.B: SA nodal artery and AV nodal artery, both typically branches of the RCA in right-dominant circulation
options.C: Circumflex artery supplies both nodes exclusively
options.D: Posterior descending artery supplies only the bundle of His

questions.explanation: In right coronary dominance (~70% of individuals), the SA nodal artery arises from the proximal RCA and the AV nodal artery from the posterior descending branch of the RCA. Proximal RCA occlusion in this setting causes inferior wall MI with sinus bradycardia (SA node ischaemia) and AV conduction delay (AV node ischaemia).

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question_text: During a radical hysterectomy, the uterine artery is ligated near the cervix. The ureter is at highest risk at this point because of which anatomical relationship, commonly remembered by a mnemonic?

options.A: The ureter passes posterior to the uterine artery throughout the pelvis
options.B: The uterine artery crosses anterior to the ureter approximately 1-2 cm lateral to the cervix — 'water under the bridge'
options.C: The ureter runs medial to the uterine artery at the pelvic brim only
options.D: There is no consistent relationship between the two structures

questions.explanation: The uterine artery crosses anteriorly over the ureter approximately 1-2 cm lateral to the cervix, at the level of the uterine isthmus — the mnemonic is 'water (ureter) under the bridge (uterine artery).' This is the most common site of ureteric injury during hysterectomy, and the ureter must be visualised and protected before the uterine artery is ligated.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question_text: A patient sustains a posterior knee dislocation in a road traffic accident and subsequently develops foot drop with sensory loss over the dorsum of the foot. Which nerve, given its fixed course, is most vulnerable in this injury?

options.A: Tibial nerve
options.B: Common peroneal (fibular) nerve, as it winds superficially around the neck of the fibula
options.C: Saphenous nerve
options.D: Femoral nerve

questions.explanation: The common peroneal (fibular) nerve winds superficially and subcutaneously around the neck of the fibula, making it highly vulnerable to traction injury in posterior knee dislocation or direct trauma at the fibular neck. Injury causes foot drop (loss of dorsiflexion and eversion) and sensory loss over the dorsum of the foot and lateral leg.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question_text: A 45-year-old male presents with severe, lancinating facial pain triggered by chewing and brushing teeth, confined to the maxillary and mandibular distribution. MRI shows a vascular loop compressing the trigeminal nerve as shown. At which specific site is compression most likely to produce trigeminal neuralgia?

options.A: The trigeminal ganglion in Meckel's cave
options.B: The root entry zone at the mid-pons, where central myelin transitions to peripheral myelin
options.C: The infraorbital foramen
options.D: The superior orbital fissure

questions.explanation: The trigeminal nerve's root entry zone (REZ) at the mid-pons — where oligodendrocyte (central) myelin transitions to Schwann cell (peripheral) myelin — is the most vulnerable site for vascular compression, typically by the superior cerebellar artery or an AICA loop. Pulsatile compression here causes trigeminal neuralgia; microvascular decompression (Jannetta procedure) at this site is the definitive surgical treatment.
questions.image_title: MRI Brain — High-Resolution Axial View at Pontine Level
key_findings: A vascular loop is seen in close contact with the trigeminal nerve at its origin from the pons
There is a visible indentation/distortion of the nerve at the root entry zone
No mass lesion or demyelinating plaque is identified at this level
The contralateral trigeminal nerve root entry zone appears normal for comparison

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question_text: A 60-year-old man with portal hypertension from cirrhosis develops dilated, tortuous periumbilical veins radiating outward from the umbilicus, with blood flow away from the umbilicus in both directions. Which veins are responsible for this 'caput medusae'?

options.A: Superficial epigastric veins draining solely into the femoral vein
options.B: Paraumbilical veins in the falciform ligament, connecting the portal vein to superior and inferior epigastric veins
options.C: Internal thoracic veins alone
options.D: Renal veins via the left gonadal vein

questions.explanation: Paraumbilical veins travel within the falciform ligament, connecting the left branch of the portal vein to periumbilical subcutaneous veins. In portal hypertension, reversed flow through these veins drains both upward into the superior epigastric/internal thoracic system and downward into the inferior epigastric/femoral system, producing the radiating centrifugal pattern of caput medusae.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question_text: A patient undergoing oesophagectomy has the thoracic duct identified and protected during dissection. At which vertebral level does the thoracic duct typically cross from the right side to the left side of the midline in the thorax?

options.A: T2-T3
options.B: T4-T5

questions.explanation: The thoracic duct ascends on the right side of the vertebral bodies in the lower thorax, then crosses to the left at approximately the T4-T5 level (behind the oesophagus), continuing upward to drain into the venous angle formed by the left internal jugular and left subclavian veins in the neck.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question_text: A 50-year-old woman undergoes axillary lymph node dissection for breast cancer staging. Post-operatively she has a winged scapula that worsens when pushing against a wall. Which nerve, running on the surface of a specific muscle, was likely injured?

options.A: Thoracodorsal nerve, supplying latissimus dorsi
options.B: Long thoracic nerve, supplying serratus anterior
options.C: Medial pectoral nerve, supplying pectoralis minor
options.D: Suprascapular nerve, supplying supraspinatus

questions.explanation: The long thoracic nerve (C5-C7) runs along the surface of serratus anterior on the medial wall of the axilla, making it vulnerable during axillary dissection. Serratus anterior anchors the scapula to the chest wall; its paralysis produces a winged scapula, most evident when pushing against resistance (e.g., a wall) due to unopposed action of the rhomboids.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question_text: A neonate fails to pass meconium, develops progressive abdominal distension, and rectal biopsy shows absent ganglion cells in the myenteric and submucosal plexuses of the distal bowel. This is Hirschsprung's disease. What is the embryological mechanism?

options.A: Failure of recanalisation of a solid-cord stage in the bowel
options.B: Failure of craniocaudal migration of vagal neural crest cells into the developing hindgut
options.C: Malrotation of the midgut around the superior mesenteric artery
options.D: Persistence of the cloacal membrane

questions.explanation: Hirschsprung's disease results from failure of neural crest cells to complete their normal craniocaudal migration into the hindgut during weeks 5-12 of gestation. The resulting aganglionic segment (always including the internal anal sphincter) cannot relax, causing a functional obstruction with massive proximal dilatation. Short-segment (rectosigmoid) involvement is most common.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question_text: A 70-year-old female with osteoporosis sustains a displaced intracapsular fracture of the femoral neck. The orthopaedic team chooses hemiarthroplasty over internal fixation due to high risk of avascular necrosis. Which vessels are torn at the fracture site, explaining this risk?

options.A: Obturator artery branches in the ligamentum teres
options.B: Retinacular arteries, branches of the medial circumflex femoral artery, running along the femoral neck within the synovial reflection
options.C: Perforating branches of the profunda femoris in the shaft
options.D: Lateral circumflex femoral artery branches in the anterior capsule

questions.explanation: The femoral head in adults receives the majority of its blood supply from retinacular arteries, branches of the medial circumflex femoral artery, which ascend along the femoral neck within the synovial (capsular) reflection. A displaced intracapsular fracture tears these vessels at the fracture site before they reach the head, explaining the 15-35% incidence of avascular necrosis.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question_text: A patient undergoes parotidectomy for a benign tumour. The surgeon carefully dissects to preserve a nerve that runs through the substance of the gland without supplying it. Which nerve is this, and what does it innervate?

options.A: Glossopharyngeal nerve — supplies the parotid gland itself
options.B: Facial nerve — passes through the gland, dividing it into superficial and deep lobes, and supplies the muscles of facial expression
options.C: Auriculotemporal nerve — carries secretomotor fibres to the parotid
options.D: Greater auricular nerve — supplies sensation to the skin overlying the parotid

questions.explanation: The facial nerve (CN VII) passes through the substance of the parotid gland, conventionally dividing it into superficial and deep lobes, without supplying the gland itself (parotid secretomotor supply comes from the glossopharyngeal nerve via the otic ganglion and auriculotemporal nerve). Preserving the facial nerve and its branches is the single most critical surgical priority during parotidectomy.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question_text: A patient undergoes appendicectomy via a Lanz (gridiron) incision in the right iliac fossa. Which muscle layer of the anterior abdominal wall is NOT encountered during this approach, distinguishing it from a midline incision?

options.A: External oblique aponeurosis
options.B: Internal oblique muscle
options.C: Rectus abdominis
options.D: Transversus abdominis

questions.explanation: The Lanz/gridiron incision passes through external oblique aponeurosis, internal oblique, and transversus abdominis (the latter two split in the direction of their fibres), then transversalis fascia and peritoneum. The rectus abdominis, lying medially within its sheath, is not encountered in this lateral muscle-splitting approach, which is the key advantage over a midline incision in terms of reduced bleeding and faster recovery.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question_text: A 52-year-old male undergoes open repair of an infrarenal AAA. Post-operatively he develops retrograde ejaculation. Damage to which structure during retroperitoneal dissection best explains this complication?

options.A: Pelvic splanchnic nerves (S2-S4, parasympathetic)
options.B: Superior hypogastric plexus and hypogastric nerves (sympathetic), anterior to the aortic bifurcation
options.C: Pudendal nerve
options.D: Genitofemoral nerve

questions.explanation: The superior hypogastric plexus and hypogastric nerves, lying anterior to the aortic bifurcation and to the left of the inferior mesenteric artery, carry sympathetic fibres that coordinate bladder neck closure and seminal vesicle/vas deferens contraction during ejaculation. Injury during retroperitoneal dissection prevents bladder neck closure, causing semen to pass retrograde into the bladder.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question_text: A patient with chronic liver disease undergoes endoscopy showing grade III oesophageal varices at the gastro-oesophageal junction. Which portosystemic anastomosis is responsible for these varices?

options.A: Superior rectal vein with middle/inferior rectal veins
options.B: Left gastric (coronary) vein with oesophageal tributaries of the azygos vein
options.C: Paraumbilical veins with superficial epigastric veins
options.D: Splenic vein with left renal vein directly

questions.explanation: Portal hypertension distends the portosystemic anastomosis at the lower oesophagus, where the left gastric (coronary) vein — a portal tributary — communicates with oesophageal tributaries of the azygos/hemiazygos veins (systemic). This is the most clinically significant portosystemic anastomosis due to the risk of life-threatening variceal haemorrhage.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question_text: A 40-year-old male with a fracture of the medial epicondyle of the humerus develops weakness of finger abduction/adduction and sensory loss over the medial one and a half fingers. Where is the nerve most vulnerable at this level, and why?

options.A: Median nerve, compressed within the carpal tunnel
options.B: Ulnar nerve, passing through the cubital tunnel posterior to the medial epicondyle, where it is superficial and unprotected by muscle
options.C: Radial nerve, compressed in the radial tunnel
options.D: Musculocutaneous nerve, piercing coracobrachialis

questions.explanation: The ulnar nerve passes posterior to the medial epicondyle through the cubital tunnel, where it is superficial and vulnerable to direct trauma or fracture-related injury. This produces weakness of the interossei and medial two lumbricals (loss of finger abduction/adduction) and sensory loss over the medial one and a half digits — the most common site of ulnar nerve compression in the upper limb.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question_text: A 40-year-old male presents with right iliac fossa pain, low-grade fever, and a positive psoas sign. CT shows the findings depicted. He has a history of treated pulmonary tuberculosis. Why does the resulting cold abscess track to the femoral triangle rather than pointing in the iliac fossa?

options.A: The psoas is enclosed within a tight fascial sheath extending from its vertebral origin to its insertion at the lesser trochanter, directing pus along this closed compartment
options.B: Lymphatic drainage of the psoas is directly to the inguinal nodes
options.C: The femoral artery carries the infection distally
options.D: Gravity alone explains the tracking, with no fascial role

questions.explanation: The psoas major is enclosed by the psoas (iliac) fascia, forming a closed compartment from its vertebral origin (T12-L5) to its insertion at the lesser trochanter, passing beneath the inguinal ligament. Pus from a vertebral (Pott's) abscess tracks along this fascial sheath, bypassing the iliac fossa entirely and pointing in the femoral triangle — the classic 'pointing' site of a psoas cold abscess.
questions.image_title: CT Abdomen and Pelvis — Coronal View
key_findings: A hypodense collection is seen within the right psoas major muscle, extending from L3 to the level of the lesser trochanter
There is associated destruction of the adjacent L3 vertebral body endplate
The collection tracks along the expected course of the psoas fascia without pointing anteriorly in the iliac fossa
No discrete abscess is identified superficial to the iliacus in the iliac fossa itself

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question_text: A footballer sustains a forced valgus injury to the knee with external rotation of the tibia. MRI confirms tears of the ACL and MCL, plus a bucket-handle tear of a third structure firmly attached to the deep surface of the MCL. Which structure completes this 'unhappy triad'?

options.A: Lateral meniscus
options.B: Medial meniscus
options.C: Posterior cruciate ligament
options.D: Lateral collateral ligament

questions.explanation: O'Donoghue's unhappy triad consists of ACL, MCL, and medial meniscus injury, classically from valgus stress combined with external rotation in contact sports. The medial meniscus is firmly attached to the deep surface of the MCL, making it vulnerable to combined injury when the MCL tears; the lateral meniscus is more mobile and less commonly involved in this mechanism.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question_text: A 67-year-old presents with sudden painless monocular visual loss described as a 'curtain coming down,' with a cherry-red spot at the fovea on fundoscopy. The occluded artery is a branch of which vessel, and where does it enter the optic nerve?

options.A: Posterior cerebral artery — enters via the optic chiasm
options.B: Ophthalmic artery — the central retinal artery pierces the dural sheath of the optic nerve about 1-1.5 cm behind the globe
options.C: Middle cerebral artery — enters at the optic canal
options.D: Internal carotid artery directly, bypassing the ophthalmic artery

questions.explanation: The central retinal artery is the first branch of the ophthalmic artery (itself the first intracranial branch of the internal carotid artery). It pierces the dural sheath of the optic nerve roughly 1-1.5 cm behind the globe and runs within the nerve to supply the inner two-thirds of the retina. Occlusion (CRAO) causes sudden painless monocular loss, with the cherry-red spot reflecting preserved choroidal perfusion of the thin foveal retina against the ischaemic surrounding retina.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question_text: A 25-year-old phenotypic female with primary amenorrhoea is found to have a 46,XY karyotype, absent uterus and fallopian tubes, a blind-ending vagina, and bilateral undescended testes. This is complete androgen insensitivity syndrome. Why are the Müllerian derivatives absent despite a non-functional androgen receptor?

options.A: Sertoli cells produce normal anti-Müllerian hormone (AMH), which is unaffected by the androgen receptor mutation and causes Müllerian duct regression
options.B: Absent testosterone production causes Müllerian regression
options.C: Leydig cells fail to develop, removing the stimulus for Müllerian persistence
options.D: The SRY gene is non-functional, preventing Müllerian duct formation entirely

questions.explanation: In complete androgen insensitivity syndrome, the testes are present and functional — Sertoli cells secrete normal AMH (independent of the androgen receptor pathway), causing complete Müllerian duct regression (absent uterus, tubes, upper vagina). Leydig cells also produce normal or elevated testosterone, but the androgen receptor mutation renders target tissues unresponsive, so Wolffian duct derivatives also fail to develop, and external genitalia default to female.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question_text: A 28-year-old female with an ectopic pregnancy in the right fallopian tube ruptures, causing haemoperitoneum. She reports pain radiating to the right shoulder tip when lying flat. Which nerve mediates this referred pain, and why?

options.A: Intercostobrachial nerve, sharing the T2 dermatome with the medial arm
options.B: Phrenic nerve (C3-C5), as blood pooling under the diaphragm irritates its peritoneal surface, with C4 sharing a dermatome with the shoulder tip
options.C: Femoral nerve, compressed by pelvic haematoma
options.D: Ilioinguinal nerve, sharing L1 innervation with the uterus

questions.explanation: Supine positioning allows intraperitoneal blood to pool beneath the right hemidiaphragm, irritating its peritoneal surface. The phrenic nerve (C3-C5) supplies the central diaphragm, and the C4 dermatome is shared with the shoulder tip (via supraclavicular nerves), producing referred shoulder-tip pain (Kehr's sign) — a classic indicator of haemoperitoneum.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question_text: A 65-year-old male has avascular necrosis of the right femoral head. The arteriogram shown demonstrates stenosis of the dominant arterial supply to the femoral head in adults. Through which anatomical route does this artery travel to reach the head?

options.A: Through the obturator foramen with the obturator nerve
options.B: Via the ligamentum teres through the acetabular notch
options.C: Posterosuperiorly around the femoral neck within the synovial reflection, deep to the short external rotators
options.D: Directly through the femoral shaft via perforating branches

questions.explanation: The medial circumflex femoral artery (a branch of the profunda femoris) is the dominant supply to the adult femoral head. It courses posteriorly between pectineus and iliopsoas, then winds around the femoral neck deep to the short external rotators before entering the synovial reflection as retinacular vessels. Displaced femoral neck fractures and posterior hip dislocations disrupt this artery, causing avascular necrosis; the ligamentum teres artery is functionally negligible in adults.
questions.image_title: Digital Subtraction Angiogram — Right Hip, Selective Femoral Injection
key_findings: The femoral artery and profunda femoris branches are well opacified
Significant narrowing is seen at the origin of the medial circumflex femoral artery
Reduced contrast filling is noted in the small vessels supplying the femoral head region
Collateral vessels are visible attempting to bridge the stenotic segment

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question_text: A neonate presents with bilious vomiting and a 'double bubble' sign on abdominal X-ray, with complete obstruction confirmed at the second part of the duodenum. What is the embryological basis of duodenal atresia?

options.A: Failure of recanalisation of the duodenum after its solid-cord stage
options.B: Malrotation with Ladd's bands compressing the duodenum
options.C: Failure of lateral body wall fold fusion
options.D: Abnormal vitelline duct obliteration

questions.explanation: Duodenal atresia results from failure of recanalisation during the solid-cord stage of duodenal development in weeks 8-10 of gestation. Obstruction at the second part (near the ampulla of Vater) produces bile-stained vomiting and the classic double-bubble sign (gas-filled stomach and proximal duodenum). It is associated with Down syndrome in approximately 30% of cases.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question_text: A 35-year-old presents with anterior chest discomfort and is found to have an anterior mediastinal mass on CT. He also has bilateral ptosis, fatigable weakness, and positive acetylcholine receptor antibodies. What is the most likely diagnosis, and what is the definitive management?

options.A: Thymoma — thymectomy is both diagnostic and potentially curative for the associated myasthenia gravis
options.B: Teratoma — surgical excision with no effect on myasthenia
options.C: Lymphoma — chemotherapy alone
options.D: Bronchogenic cyst — observation only

questions.explanation: Anterior mediastinal masses in adults with myasthenia gravis and positive AChR antibodies strongly suggest thymoma (the classic 4 T's of anterior mediastinal masses: thymoma, teratoma, terrible lymphoma, thyroid). Thymoma is found in 10-15% of MG patients, and thymectomy induces remission or improvement in the majority of MG patients with an associated thymoma.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question_text: A patient with a stab wound to the posterior triangle of the neck, at the level of the middle third of sternocleidomastoid, develops inability to shrug the right shoulder and weakness of trapezius. Which nerve was injured, given its superficial course in this triangle?

options.A: Phrenic nerve
options.B: Spinal accessory nerve (CN XI)
options.C: Long thoracic nerve
options.D: Suprascapular nerve

questions.explanation: The spinal accessory nerve (CN XI) crosses the posterior triangle of the neck superficially, from the posterior border of sternocleidomastoid to the anterior border of trapezius, making it the most exposed nerve in this region and highly vulnerable to penetrating trauma. Injury causes weakness of shoulder shrugging (trapezius) and head turning (sternocleidomastoid).

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question_text: During a pancreaticoduodenectomy (Whipple's procedure), the surgeon must identify hepatic arterial anatomy before resection. The most common arterial variant, if missed, can cause right lobe hepatic ischaemia despite a patent proper hepatic artery. What is this variant?

options.A: Replaced right hepatic artery arising from the superior mesenteric artery, running posterior to the portal vein
options.B: Replaced left hepatic artery from the left gastric artery
options.C: Accessory cystic artery from the gastroduodenal artery
options.D: Absent coeliac trunk with direct aortic branches

questions.explanation: A replaced (aberrant) right hepatic artery arising from the SMA is the most common hepatic arterial variant (occurring in roughly 15-20% of individuals). It runs posterior to the portal vein and lateral to the bile duct. Failure to identify this vessel before SMA-related dissection in a Whipple's procedure risks its inadvertent division, causing right lobe ischaemia even though the proper hepatic artery (supplying the left lobe in this variant) remains patent.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question_text: A patient undergoes total thyroidectomy and develops post-operative hoarseness, worse on phonation, with the right vocal cord fixed in a paramedian position on laryngoscopy. Which nerve was most likely injured?

options.A: External branch of the superior laryngeal nerve
options.B: Recurrent laryngeal nerve
options.C: Internal branch of the superior laryngeal nerve
options.D: Glossopharyngeal nerve

questions.explanation: The recurrent laryngeal nerve supplies all intrinsic laryngeal muscles except cricothyroid and provides sensation below the vocal cords. Injury produces ipsilateral vocal cord paralysis, with the cord fixed in a paramedian position due to unopposed cricothyroid tone. The external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve supplies cricothyroid alone; its injury causes loss of high-pitch phonation without cord paralysis.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question_text: A preterm neonate is found to have a continuous machine-like murmur loudest at the left second intercostal space, confirmed as patent ductus arteriosus on echocardiography. The ductus arteriosus is the persistent remnant of which embryological structure?

options.A: Left third aortic arch
options.B: Left sixth aortic arch (distal portion)
options.C: Right fourth aortic arch
options.D: Truncus arteriosus directly

questions.explanation: The ductus arteriosus develops from the distal portion of the left sixth aortic arch, connecting the pulmonary trunk to the descending aorta. The proximal part of the same arch forms the left pulmonary artery. Normal closure occurs within 24-48 hours of birth due to rising arterial oxygen tension and falling prostaglandin levels; prematurity delays this maturation, predisposing to PDA.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question_text: A 35-year-old male sustains a posterior dislocation of the hip in a road traffic accident, presenting with a shortened, internally rotated, adducted limb and subsequent foot drop. Which nerve division is more vulnerable in this injury, and why?

options.A: Tibial division — runs more medially and is more tethered
options.B: Common peroneal division — runs more laterally with less redundancy, closer to the displaced femoral head
options.C: Femoral nerve — directly compressed anteriorly
options.D: Obturator nerve — stretched during dislocation

questions.explanation: Posterior hip dislocation stretches the sciatic nerve as it exits below piriformis. The common peroneal (fibular) division is more vulnerable than the tibial division because it runs more laterally, closer to the displaced femoral head, and has less fascicular redundancy to absorb traction — producing the characteristic foot drop seen after this injury.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question_text: A 65-year-old male with prostate carcinoma presents with low back pain and is found to have lytic vertebral metastases at L4 without pulmonary metastases. Which venous route explains the characteristic spread of prostate cancer to the vertebrae, bypassing the lungs?

options.A: Systemic arterial spread via the lumbar arteries
options.B: Batson's vertebral venous plexus, a valveless network communicating with pelvic veins
options.C: Lymphatic spread via the thoracic duct
options.D: Direct extension through the posterior longitudinal ligament

questions.explanation: Batson's vertebral venous plexus is a valveless, low-pressure venous network surrounding the vertebral column, communicating directly with pelvic veins. Raised intra-abdominal pressure (coughing, straining) can reverse flow, allowing tumour emboli from pelvic organs (prostate, bladder, uterus) to seed the vertebral column directly without first passing through the pulmonary circulation, explaining vertebral metastasis in the absence of lung involvement.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question_text: A 45-year-old woman with breast cancer in the upper outer quadrant undergoes sentinel lymph node biopsy. To which group of axillary nodes does the primary drainage of this quadrant proceed first?

options.A: Internal mammary nodes
options.B: Anterior (pectoral) group of axillary nodes — level I
options.C: Apical (subclavicular) nodes — level III, directly
options.D: Supraclavicular nodes

questions.explanation: The breast drains predominantly to axillary lymph nodes, with the anterior (pectoral) group at level I (lateral to pectoralis minor) receiving the primary drainage from all quadrants, including the upper outer quadrant where most breast cancers arise. Level II and III nodes represent secondary echelons; skip metastases directly to level III are rare.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question_text: A neonate is born with anencephaly, and the mother had a markedly elevated second-trimester maternal serum alpha-fetoprotein. Failure of which embryological event, and at what gestational week, explains this defect?

options.A: Failure of the caudal neuropore to close by day 28
options.B: Failure of the cranial neuropore to close by day 24-26 (week 4)
options.C: Failure of neural crest cell migration at week 6
options.D: Failure of pontine flexure formation at week 8

questions.explanation: Anencephaly results from failure of the cranial neuropore to close by day 24-26 of development, exposing the developing forebrain to amniotic fluid and causing its destruction. Elevated maternal AFP, leaking from exposed neural tissue, is the key biochemical screening marker. Failure of the caudal neuropore (closes by day 28) instead causes spina bifida. Periconceptional folic acid reduces the risk of all neural tube defects.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question_text: A 55-year-old male presents with right leg pain in an L4 dermatomal distribution, an absent right knee jerk, and quadriceps weakness. The myelogram shown confirms a disc prolapse at L4-L5. Which nerve root is compressed, and why is it not the L4 root that exits at that same level?

options.A: L5 nerve root — the traversing root, descending obliquely across the L4-L5 disc before exiting one level below at the L5-S1 foramen
options.B: L4 nerve root — directly compressed by the disc at the same level it exits
options.C: L3 nerve root — from far-lateral disc extrusion
options.D: S1 nerve root — from downward migration of a sequestered fragment

questions.explanation: Each lumbar nerve root exits beneath the pedicle of its own numbered vertebra (the L4 root exits at the L4-L5 foramen). A posterolateral disc prolapse at L4-L5, however, compresses the traversing L5 root, which descends obliquely across the disc before exiting one level lower. L5 root compression causes sensory loss over the L5 dermatome and weak ankle dorsiflexion, with a NORMAL knee jerk (mediated by L4) — distinguishing it from an L4 radiculopathy.
key_findings: Contrast outlines the subarachnoid space down to the conus medullaris at the L1-L2 level
Multiple thin filling defects below this level represent the cauda equina nerve roots
A rounded filling defect approximately 1.5 cm in diameter is present at L4-L5, compressing the right side of the dural sac
The remainder of the contrast column below the lesion appears preserved

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question_text: A patient undergoes ERCP with sphincterotomy for a common bile duct stone and subsequently develops acute pancreatitis. Which anatomical mechanism most directly explains this common complication?

options.A: Reflux of duodenal contents through the disrupted sphincter of Oddi
options.B: Hydrostatic injection of contrast under pressure directly into the main pancreatic duct, causing ductal hypertension and acinar injury
options.C: Thermal injury from the sphincterotome propagating to the pancreatic parenchyma
options.D: Inadvertent cannulation of the minor papilla alone

questions.explanation: Post-ERCP pancreatitis is most commonly caused by hydrostatic injury from contrast or saline injected under pressure directly into the main pancreatic duct, causing ductal hypertension and premature intra-acinar activation of trypsinogen. Risk factors include difficult papillary cannulation, repeated pancreatic duct opacification, and sphincter of Oddi dysfunction; rectal indomethacin reduces incidence significantly.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question_text: A 28-year-old male presents with severe unilateral periorbital headache, ptosis, and a fixed dilated pupil. Imaging confirms an aneurysm at the junction of the internal carotid artery and the posterior communicating artery, compressing the third cranial nerve. Why does this compression preferentially affect the pupil?

options.A: The pupilloconstrictor parasympathetic fibres run superficially in the dorsomedial aspect of CN III, making them vulnerable to external compression before the deeper motor fibres
options.B: The pupil fibres run centrally and are protected from external compression
options.C: Pupillary involvement reflects ischaemia rather than compression
options.D: The aneurysm directly compresses the Edinger-Westphal nucleus in the midbrain

questions.explanation: The parasympathetic pupilloconstrictor fibres of CN III travel superficially in the dorsomedial aspect of the nerve, making them the first to be affected by external compression (e.g., from an expanding aneurysm), producing a 'surgical' pupil-involving palsy. In contrast, ischaemic CN III palsy (e.g., diabetic microangiopathy) typically affects the deeper core motor fibres while sparing the superficial parasympathetic fibres, producing a pupil-sparing palsy — a key clinical distinction.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question_text: A 30-year-old undergoes ureteroscopy for a stone at the junction of the upper and middle thirds of the ureter. Which direction should periureteric tissue be preserved to avoid devascularising the ureter at this level?

options.A: Medial tissue, since the upper ureter is supplied medially from the aorta and renal artery
options.B: Lateral tissue exclusively, throughout the ureter's length
options.C: No specific orientation matters, since the ureter is avascular and relies on diffusion
options.D: Anterior tissue only

questions.explanation: The ureter has a segmental blood supply: the upper third is supplied medially from the renal artery and aorta, while the lower third is supplied laterally from the internal iliac, uterine, and vesical vessels. Excessive skeletonisation that disregards this medial-to-lateral transition risks ischaemic stricture, the most common cause of post-operative ureteric complications.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question_text: A 44-year-old male with coarctation of the aorta just distal to the left subclavian artery has prominent bilateral rib notching on chest X-ray along the inferior margins of ribs 3-8. Which vessels cause this notching?

options.A: Dilated azygos and hemiazygos veins
options.B: Dilated, tortuous posterior intercostal arteries acting as collaterals around the coarctation
options.C: Dilated internal mammary arteries causing anterior notching
options.D: Subclavian artery dilatation alone

questions.explanation: In post-ductal coarctation, collateral flow bypasses the obstruction via subclavian → internal mammary → anterior intercostal → posterior intercostal → descending aorta pathways. The posterior intercostal arteries (ribs 3-8; ribs 1-2 have separate supply from the costocervical trunk) become markedly dilated and tortuous from years of increased retrograde flow, eroding the costal groove and producing the classic bilateral rib notching.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question_text: A neonate with Kartagener's syndrome has dextrocardia with situs inversus, bronchiectasis, and immotile sperm, with absent dynein arms in cilia on electron microscopy. Through which mechanism does the underlying ciliary defect cause situs inversus?

options.A: Failure of the primitive streak to establish a left-right axis directly
options.B: Failure of leftward nodal cilia flow to establish left-sided identity signals (Nodal, Lefty, Pitx2), randomising organ laterality
options.C: Abnormal neural crest migration determining laterality
options.D: Absent FGF8 signalling preventing rightward cardiac looping

questions.explanation: Left-right asymmetry is established at the embryonic node by motile cilia generating a leftward flow that activates Nodal signalling, restricted to the left side by Lefty-1, leading to Pitx2 expression and left-sided organ identity. In primary ciliary dyskinesia (Kartagener's syndrome), immotile nodal cilia abolish this directional flow, randomising laterality determination — roughly half of affected individuals develop situs inversus totalis, while the rest retain normal situs.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question_text: A 62-year-old undergoes an Ivor Lewis oesophagectomy with thoracic duct ligation at T8 to prevent chyle leak. Despite this, he develops a right chylothorax post-operatively. Which anatomical variant best explains why ligation at T8 failed?

options.A: The thoracic duct crossed to the left above T8, so chyle from the upper duct drained into the right pleural space via an unligated segment
options.B: A right-sided accessory or duplicated thoracic duct bypassed the single ligation site and continued draining into the right pleural space
options.C: Chylothorax is unrelated to the thoracic duct in this case
options.D: The thoracic duct has no anatomical variation, so the ligature must have failed mechanically

questions.explanation: The thoracic duct shows considerable anatomical variation, with accessory ducts, duplications, or right-sided branches present in a substantial proportion of individuals. A right-sided accessory duct can bypass a single ligation point at T8 and continue draining lymph into the right pleural space. For this reason, mass ligation of all retroperitoneal/mediastinal tissue between the aorta, oesophagus, and azygos vein at the diaphragmatic hiatus is considered more reliable than isolated single-duct ligation.
key_findings: Contrast outlines the main thoracic duct ascending on the right side of the lower thoracic vertebral bodies
A separate, smaller accessory duct is seen running parallel to the main duct on the right side
The accessory duct continues independently toward the right pleural space, bypassing the level of surgical ligation
The main duct shows normal crossing to the left at the expected mid-thoracic level

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question_text: A patient undergoes left hepatectomy for hepatocellular carcinoma. Pre-operative volumetry showed the future liver remnant (right lobe) at 28% of total liver volume, the lower limit for a non-cirrhotic liver. On day 3, he develops ascites, coagulopathy, and rising bilirubin — post-hepatectomy liver failure. What is the underlying mechanism?

options.A: Portal vein thrombosis unrelated to remnant size
options.B: 'Small-for-size syndrome' — the inadequate remnant receives the full portal flow, causing portal hyperperfusion, sinusoidal shear injury, and hepatocyte dysfunction
options.C: Direct surgical injury to the remnant parenchyma
options.D: Pre-existing cirrhosis unrelated to the resection

questions.explanation: Post-hepatectomy liver failure occurs when the remnant liver is insufficient for the body's metabolic and haemodynamic demands. Minimum safe future liver remnant thresholds are approximately 25-30% for a non-cirrhotic liver, 30% for a steatotic liver, and 40% for a cirrhotic liver. When the remnant is at or below this threshold, it receives the entire portal venous flow previously shared with the resected lobe, causing portal hyperperfusion and sinusoidal injury — 'small-for-size syndrome.' Pre-operative portal vein embolisation can induce contralateral hypertrophy to mitigate this risk before major hepatectomy.
